questions.a: A simplified picture of a real system that keeps its essential features and drops unimportant details so it can be studied easily.

questions.q: Why do scientists use models although they are not exact?
questions.a: Models make complex systems manageable; predictions from a good model can be tested and the model improved.

questions.q: Give one example of a model used in science.
questions.a: The ball-and-stick model of a molecule, or a model of the solar system - both simplify reality to show key relationships.
A unit agreed upon internationally that never changes with place or person, like the metre or kilogram.

questions.q: What does SI stand for and why was it adopted?
questions.a: Systeme International - a single accepted set of units so that measurements mean the same everywhere.

questions.q: Name the SI units of length, mass and time.
How does a scientific law differ from a theory?
questions.a: A law states what always happens (often as an equation); a theory explains why it happens and can be revised with new evidence.

questions.q: What makes a statement a scientific principle?
questions.a: It is a basic rule drawn from repeated experiments that holds without exception in its range, like Archimedes' principle.

questions.q: Can a theory be discarded? When?
questions.a: Yes - when new experiments show results the theory cannot explain, it is modified or replaced.
It is based on measurable variables and can be tested by experiment, so it could turn out wrong.

questions.q: Why is testability important in science?
questions.a: A claim that no test could disprove is outside science; testability lets evidence settle the question.

questions.q: Give an example of a testable prediction.
questions.a: 'If plants get more sunlight, they will grow taller in two weeks' - it names measurable quantities and can be checked.
